meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Why did Owen's grade drop to a zero on his Hamlet essay?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
A machine's guess. The company that sells it says it shouldn't be the only basis for punishing a student. What else do you have?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Now what do you have besides the score?

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing those times down. Did you show this to Owen before you entered the zero?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Kids misquote plays all the time. I'm reading 3.2 now, and you still haven't said whether Owen was asked about any of this before the zero.
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Students change their argument between an outline and an essay. That's called writing. Is there anything else, or is this all of it?

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.
A forty-minute piece under a clock isn't a weekend essay. I want all of it in writing tonight, the notes included. Whatever happens next, it stays off his record, and it stays quiet.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.
Okay. A private rewrite, its mark replaces the zero, nothing on his record, in writing tonight. I'll take it to put this behind him, Hale, and anything else I want goes in my email.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Thursday, November 12, after school. Put that date in the email with the rest.
Do we have an agreement?
Yes: a private supervised rewrite Thursday, November 12, its mark replacing the zero, nothing on his record, all of it in writing tonight.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, after school, its mark replacing the zero and nothing going on Owen's record. I still want every document you showed me, including your notes from November 2, sent to me in writing. I expect the agreement in writing tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: Last position: she accepted a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, and she still wants your documents and the agreement in writing; that is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, and her time did not run out first.
What moved her: You answered her paste-it-from-elsewhere defence before she raised it, with a misquoted line she could check against the play herself, because a document she can verify is the only thing she trusts.
What cost ground: You opened with the checker score, which cost you because she cannot check it and the company that sells it says it should not stand alone.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history, with its late-night edit times, came close to that kind of night, and it proves nothing about the essay, it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: Open with your ownership of the early zero and your first dated document, and leave the checker score out entirely.
